::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Paper.** Author A, Author B, Author C. *Title of the paper.* Journal
volume:pages (year). [doi:10.xxxx/yyyyy](https://doi.org/10.xxxx/yyyyy)

**Presented by** Presenter Name · **1 January 2026**
:::

## The study

What the paper set out to do, what they did, and what they found. Two or three
paragraphs. Enough that someone who has not read it can follow the discussion
below.

## Discussion

Sections from here follow the shape of the actual discussion — there is no fixed
template. Common ones are "Criticisms", "Terminology clarified in discussion", or
a heading naming the single argument that dominated.

Write narrative prose, not bullet-point minutes. Capture the *argument*: the
objection someone raised, why it mattered, and whether it survived. Record
disagreement that was left unresolved — it is more useful than a tidy consensus
nobody actually reached.

Name the presenter and anyone who proposed follow-up reading. Attribute other
points impersonally: "it was noted", "one attendee argued".

Criticise the work, not the authors.

::: {.content-hidden}
Figures: only your own, or from an open-access paper under a CC licence with
attribution. Never screenshot a figure from a paywalled paper. Describing it in
prose is usually enough. See contributing.qmd#figures.

Note: this block is `.content-hidden`, so it never reaches the rendered page.
Plain `<!-- HTML comments -->` DO appear in the page source — don't use them for
anything you would not publish.
:::

## Follow-up reading

Anything the room suggested reading next, with a full citation and DOI, and a
sentence on why it is worth reading alongside this one.
